claim: Morinda citrifolia fruit (morinda) is the sole host of Drosophila sechellia.
source: Morinda citrifolia fruit (morinda) is the sole host of Drosophila sechellia (Tsacas and Baechli, 1981), a close relative of Drosophila melanogaster and endemic to the Seychelles archipelago (Louis and David, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsacas and Baechli, 1981

claim: D. sechellia is a close relative of Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Morinda citrifolia fruit (morinda) is the sole host of Drosophila sechellia (Tsacas and Baechli, 1981), a close relative of Drosophila melanogaster and endemic to the Seychelles archipelago (Louis and David, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Louis and David, 1986

claim: D. sechellia is endemic to the Seychelles archipelago.
source: Morinda citrifolia fruit (morinda) is the sole host of Drosophila sechellia (Tsacas and Baechli, 1981), a close relative of Drosophila melanogaster and endemic to the Seychelles archipelago (Louis and David, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Louis and David, 1986

claim: Morinda fruits are toxic to all other drosophilids.
source: A peculiar aspect of the specialization is that morinda fruits are toxic to all other drosophilids (Legal et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Legal et al., 1992

claim: The toxicity of morinda stems from a high content of carboxylic acids (primarily octanoic and hexanoic acid).
source: The toxicity stems from a high content of carboxylic acids (primarily octanoic and hexanoic acid) (Legal et al., 1994), to which D. sechellia appears to be resistant (Farine et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Legal et al., 1994

claim: D. sechellia appears to be resistant to morinda carboxylic acids.
source: The toxicity stems from a high content of carboxylic acids (primarily octanoic and hexanoic acid) (Legal et al., 1994), to which D. sechellia appears to be resistant (Farine et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farine et al., 1996

claim: The chemosensory system of D. sechellia is specialized in detecting and coding key volatiles produced by morinda.
source: The chemosensory system of D. sechellia is specialized in detecting and coding key volatiles produced by morinda (Dekker et al., 2006) while devoid of the repellence towards the acids (Matsuo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dekker et al., 2006

claim: D. sechellia is devoid of the repellence towards morinda acids.
source: The chemosensory system of D. sechellia is specialized in detecting and coding key volatiles produced by morinda (Dekker et al., 2006) while devoid of the repellence towards the acids (Matsuo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsuo et al., 2007

claim: D. sechellia females exhibit a low reproductive potential, partly because of a low ovariole number and partly because of fairly low egg production.
source: On the other hand, D. sechellia females exhibit a low reproductive potential, partly because of a low ovariole number and partly because of fairly low egg production (R'Kha et al., 1991; R'kha et al., 1997), making it difficult to raise D. sechellia under laboratory conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to R'Kha et al., 1991 and R'kha et al., 1997

claim: It is difficult to raise D. sechellia under laboratory conditions.
source: On the other hand, D. sechellia females exhibit a low reproductive potential, partly because of a low ovariole number and partly because of fairly low egg production (R'Kha et al., 1991; R'kha et al., 1997), making it difficult to raise D. sechellia under laboratory conditions.
evidence: Inferred from low reproductive potential

claim: Morinda stimulates egg production in D. sechellia.
source: In turn, morinda stimulates egg production (R'kha et al., 1997), and D. sechellia clearly prefers to oviposit in medium containing morinda carboxylic acids (Amlou et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to R'kha et al., 1997

claim: D. sechellia clearly prefers to oviposit in medium containing morinda carboxylic acids.
source: In turn, morinda stimulates egg production (R'kha et al., 1997), and D. sechellia clearly prefers to oviposit in medium containing morinda carboxylic acids (Amlou et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amlou et al., 1998

claim: On its host, D. sechellia increases expression of genes involved with oogenesis and fatty acid metabolism.
source: On its host, D. sechellia increases expression of genes involved with oogenesis and fatty acid metabolism (Dworkin and Jones, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dworkin and Jones, 2009

claim: Embryonic survival in morinda is a maternally inherited trait and does not depend on the genotype of the embryo.
source: Embryonic survival in morinda is a maternally inherited trait and does not depend on the genotype of the embryo (R'Kha et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to R'Kha et al., 1991

claim: D. sechellia raised on standard diet produced few eggs compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin and D. melanogaster Canton-S.
source: In agreement with previous reports, D. sechellia raised on standard diet produced few eggs compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin and D. melanogaster Canton-S (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), raised on the same media.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the standard diet did not increase egg production in D. sechellia.
source: The addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the standard diet did not increase egg production in D. sechellia (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: D. sechellia raised on a non-host fruit (banana diet) showed a slight increase in the number of eggs laid.
source: D. sechellia raised on a non-host fruit (banana diet) showed a slight increase in the number of eggs laid (Figure 1B), but this number did not increase further with the addition of morinda carboxylic acids (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: D. sechellia raised on morinda diet showed a sixfold increase in egg production.
source: D. sechellia raised on morinda diet, however, showed a sixfold increase in egg production (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Morinda diet did not affect the number of eggs produced by D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin.
source: Morinda diet did not affect the number of eggs produced by D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin and slightly reduced those of D. melanogaster Canton-S (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as did the addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the standard diet (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Morinda diet slightly reduced egg production in D. melanogaster Canton-S.
source: Morinda diet did not affect the number of eggs produced by D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin and slightly reduced those of D. melanogaster Canton-S (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as did the addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the standard diet (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Banana tripled egg production in D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin.
source: Banana, however, tripled egg production in D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The increase in egg production from banana in D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin could be inhibited by the addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the banana.
source: This increase could be inhibited by the addition of morinda carboxylic acids to the banana (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The presence of a natural host modulates the reproductive capacity of Drosophila.
source: These results demonstrate that the presence of a natural host modulates the reproductive capacity of Drosophila.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results on egg production

claim: Morinda has a strong effect on D. sechellia egg production that goes beyond the reported stimulatory effect of the carboxylic acids on oviposition.
source: In particular, morinda has a strong effect on D. sechellia egg production that goes beyond the reported stimulatory effect of the carboxylic acids on oviposition (Amlou et al., 1998).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and comparison with citation

claim: Mated D. melanogaster females typically exhibit multiple ovarioles carrying vitellogenic cysts.
source: Mated D. melanogaster females typically exhibit multiple ovarioles carrying vitellogenic cysts (Spradling et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spradling et al., 1997

claim: Females of D. sechellia had cysts normally composed of 15 nurse cells and one oocyte, surrounded by follicular cells.
source: Females of D. sechellia had cysts normally composed of 15 nurse cells and one oocyte, surrounded by follicular cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Kept on standard diet, mated D. sechellia held oocytes in early developmental stages (<S8).
source: Kept on standard diet, mated D. sechellia held oocytes in early developmental stages (<S8) (Figure 1D) with few ovarioles, if any, carrying vitellogenic cyst (>S8), what resulted in a significantly lowered rate of vitellogenesis (calculated as >S8/<S8) in D. sechellia compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and quantification in Figure 1E

claim: D. sechellia on standard diet had a significantly lowered rate of vitellogenesis compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin.
source: Kept on standard diet, mated D. sechellia held oocytes in early developmental stages (<S8) (Figure 1D) with few ovarioles, if any, carrying vitellogenic cyst (>S8), what resulted in a significantly lowered rate of vitellogenesis (calculated as >S8/<S8) in D. sechellia compared to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The low number of ovarioles in D. sechellia was reflected in the low number of total cysts compared to in D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin.
source: The low number of ovarioles in D. sechellia (R'kha et al., 1997) was reflected in the low number of total cysts compared to in D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citation to R'kha et al., 1997

claim: The halt in oocyte development explains the low production of eggs in D. sechellia raised on standard diet.
source: The halt in oocyte development explains the low production of eggs in D. sechellia raised on standard diet.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of oocyte development and egg production

claim: D. sechellia fed on morinda diet showed a significantly increased vitellogenesis rate.
source: D. sechellia fed on morinda diet showed a significantly increased vitellogenesis rate (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E

claim: Adding the morinda carboxylic acids had no effect on vitellogenesis in D. sechellia.
source: Adding the morinda carboxylic acids, however, had no effect on vitellogenesis in D. sechellia (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: D. sechellia requires components of the morinda fruit other than just the carboxylic acids to induce vitellogenesis and increase egg production.
source: We thus conclude that D. sechellia requires components of the morinda fruit other than just the carboxylic acids to induce vitellogenesis and increase egg production.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results showing morinda effect but not carboxylic acid effect

claim: Environmental and physiological stressors can cause egg chambers in the ovaries of Drosophila to be eliminated by apoptosis at oogenesis checkpoints in region-2/3 of the germarium or cyst stage S7/S8.
source: Environmental and physiological stressors can cause egg chambers in the ovaries of Drosophila to be eliminated by apoptosis at oogenesis checkpoints in region-2/3 of the germarium or cyst stage S7/S8 (the mid-oogenesis checkpoint) (Drummond-Barbosa and Spradling, 2001; McCall, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drummond-Barbosa and Spradling, 2001 and McCall, 2004

claim: D. sechellia flies fed a standard diet showed massive apoptosis occurring at S7/S8 cysts, and to a lesser extent in region-2/3 of the germarium.
source: Flies fed a standard diet showed massive apoptosis occurring at S7/S8 cysts, and to a lesser extent in region-2/3 of the germarium (Figure 1—figure supplement 2); suggesting that apoptosis could be the reason for the depressed oviposition on standard media.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Apoptosis could be the reason for the depressed oviposition on standard media in D. sechellia.
source: Flies fed a standard diet showed massive apoptosis occurring at S7/S8 cysts, and to a lesser extent in region-2/3 of the germarium (Figure 1—figure supplement 2); suggesting that apoptosis could be the reason for the depressed oviposition on standard media.
evidence: Inferred from observation of apoptosis and low egg production

claim: D. sechellia flies fed a morinda diet showed strikingly few apoptotic cysts.
source: On the other hand, D. sechellia flies fed a morinda diet showed strikingly few apoptotic cysts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), in line with the stimulatory effect of morinda in egg-production.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Low food availability can trigger the mid-oogenesis checkpoint.
source: Low food availability can trigger the mid-oogenesis checkpoint (Terashima and Bownes, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Terashima and Bownes, 2004

claim: D. sechellia adults raised on the standard diet showed slightly higher weights than did flies raised on morinda diet.
source: In fact, D. sechellia adults raised on the standard diet showed slightly higher weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and also consumed more food than did flies raised on morinda diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: D. sechellia adults raised on the standard diet consumed more food than did flies raised on morinda diet.
source: In fact, D. sechellia adults raised on the standard diet showed slightly higher weights (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and also consumed more food than did flies raised on morinda diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The halt in oogenesis observed in D. sechellia is not a consequence of starvation or aberrant feeding behaviour.
source: Hence, we conclude that the halt in oogenesis observed in D. sechellia is not a consequence of starvation or aberrant feeding behaviour.
evidence: Inferred from weight and food consumption data

claim: Oocyte-cyst progression is under tight maternal hormonal regulation: juvenile- and steroid hormones are mutually controlled by the biogenic amine dopamine (DA), ensuring normal oogenesis.
source: Oocyte-cyst progression is under tight maternal hormonal regulation: juvenile- and steroid hormones are mutually controlled by the biogenic amine dopamine (DA), ensuring normal oogenesis (Gruntenko and Rauschenbach, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gruntenko and Rauschenbach, 2008

claim: Interruption of DA during development in D. melanogaster results in small ovaries and poor egg production.
source: Interruption of DA during development in D. melanogaster results in small ovaries and poor egg production (Neckameyer, 1996), both of which are features that characterise adult D. sechellia (R'kha et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Neckameyer, 1996 and R'kha et al., 1997

claim: Genes involved in DA differentiation were shown differentially expressed in D. sechellia compared to the generalists species D. melanogaster and the sister Drosophila simulans.
source: Moreover, genes involved in DA differentiation were shown differentially expressed in D. sechellia compared to the generalists species D. melanogaster and the sister Drosophila simulans (Dworkin and Jones, 2009; Wurmser et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dworkin and Jones, 2009 and Wurmser et al., 2011

claim: Supplementing the standard diet with the DA precursor l-DOPA significantly increased the number of eggs produced by D. sechellia.
source: Indeed, supplementing the standard diet with the DA precursor 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (l-DOPA) significantly increased the number of eggs produced by D. sechellia (Figure 2A), whereas the addition of DA itself had no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The addition of DA itself had no effect on egg production in D. sechellia.
source: Indeed, supplementing the standard diet with the DA precursor 3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine (l-DOPA) significantly increased the number of eggs produced by D. sechellia (Figure 2A), whereas the addition of DA itself had no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Adding the monoamine octopamine (OA), or its precursor tyramine (TA), did not affect egg production in D. sechellia.
source: Likewise, adding the monoamine octopamine (OA), or its precursor tyramine (TA), did not affect egg production (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: l-DOPA supplementation did not change the total number of D. sechellia oocyte-cysts.
source: l-DOPA supplementation did not change the total number of D. sechellia oocyte-cysts (p = 0.28103, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: l-DOPA supplementation drastically reduced apoptosis in the ovary of D. sechellia.
source: Instead, it drastically reduced apoptosis in the ovary (Figure 2B) increasing vitellogenesis significantly (Figure 2C), whereas DA, TA and OA had no such effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: l-DOPA supplementation increased vitellogenesis significantly in D. sechellia.
source: Instead, it drastically reduced apoptosis in the ovary (Figure 2B) increasing vitellogenesis significantly (Figure 2C), whereas DA, TA and OA had no such effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: DA, TA and OA had no effect on apoptosis or vitellogenesis in D. sechellia.
source: Instead, it drastically reduced apoptosis in the ovary (Figure 2B) increasing vitellogenesis significantly (Figure 2C), whereas DA, TA and OA had no such effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: The administration of the DA precursor l-DOPA is sufficient to stimulate oocyte progression and egg production in D. sechellia.
source: These results show that the administration of the DA precursor l-DOPA is sufficient to stimulate oocyte progression and egg production in D. sechellia.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with l-DOPA supplementation

claim: Morinda contains 180.4 ± 3.5 ng l-DOPA per gram of fruit pulp.
source: Indeed, we detected 180.4 ± 3.5 ng l-DOPA (mean ± s.e.m; N = 3) per gram of fruit pulp (Figure 2D) in morinda extracts analysed by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS).
evidence: Supported by UHPLC-MS analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: DA, OA or TA were not detected in morinda.
source: Notably, we did not detect DA, OA or TA in morinda.
evidence: Supported by UHPLC-MS analysis

claim: Unripe morinda fruits contained 150.99 ± 8 ng l-DOPA per gram of fruit.
source: Unripe (150.99 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) and overripe (147.47 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) morinda fruits contained l-DOPA in equal amounts, what suggests that oxidisation, known to occur commonly in monoamines through atmospherical exposure, is prevented in morinda.
evidence: Supported by UHPLC-MS analysis

claim: Overripe morinda fruits contained 147.47 ± 8 ng l-DOPA per gram of fruit.
source: Unripe (150.99 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) and overripe (147.47 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) morinda fruits contained l-DOPA in equal amounts, what suggests that oxidisation, known to occur commonly in monoamines through atmospherical exposure, is prevented in morinda.
evidence: Supported by UHPLC-MS analysis

claim: Oxidisation is prevented in morinda.
source: Unripe (150.99 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) and overripe (147.47 ± 8 ng l-DOPA [mean ± s.e.m; N = 3] per gram of fruit) morinda fruits contained l-DOPA in equal amounts, what suggests that oxidisation, known to occur commonly in monoamines through atmospherical exposure, is prevented in morinda.
evidence: Inferred from equal l-DOPA amounts in unripe and overripe fruits

claim: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content.
source: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content—octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity (Guo et al., 2010)—and the ensuing low pH of the fruit (4.1 ± 0.1 [N = 7] and 3.6 ± 0.1 [N = 5] [mean ± s.e.m.], ripe and overripe morinda, respectively; for comparison, 5.7 ± 0.2 [mean ± s.e.m.], [N = 4], ripe banana; p = 0.0001; one-way ANOVA), known for its antioxidant properties.
evidence: Inferred from citation and pH measurements

claim: Octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity.
source: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content—octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity (Guo et al., 2010)—and the ensuing low pH of the fruit (4.1 ± 0.1 [N = 7] and 3.6 ± 0.1 [N = 5] [mean ± s.e.m.], ripe and overripe morinda, respectively; for comparison, 5.7 ± 0.2 [mean ± s.e.m.], [N = 4], ripe banana; p = 0.0001; one-way ANOVA), known for its antioxidant properties.
evidence: Supported by citation to Guo et al., 2010

claim: Ripe morinda has a pH of 4.1 ± 0.1.
source: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content—octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity (Guo et al., 2010)—and the ensuing low pH of the fruit (4.1 ± 0.1 [N = 7] and 3.6 ± 0.1 [N = 5] [mean ± s.e.m.], ripe and overripe morinda, respectively; for comparison, 5.7 ± 0.2 [mean ± s.e.m.], [N = 4], ripe banana; p = 0.0001; one-way ANOVA), known for its antioxidant properties.
evidence: Supported by pH measurements

claim: Overripe morinda has a pH of 3.6 ± 0.1.
source: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content—octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity (Guo et al., 2010)—and the ensuing low pH of the fruit (4.1 ± 0.1 [N = 7] and 3.6 ± 0.1 [N = 5] [mean ± s.e.m.], ripe and overripe morinda, respectively; for comparison, 5.7 ± 0.2 [mean ± s.e.m.], [N = 4], ripe banana; p = 0.0001; one-way ANOVA), known for its antioxidant properties.
evidence: Supported by pH measurements

claim: Ripe banana has a pH of 5.7 ± 0.2.
source: The preservation of l-DOPA is likely due to the high carboxylic acid content—octanoic and hexanoic acids have been shown to inhibit diphenol oxidase activity (Guo et al., 2010)—and the ensuing low pH of the fruit (4.1 ± 0.1 [N = 7] and 3.6 ± 0.1 [N = 5] [mean ± s.e.m.], ripe and overripe morinda, respectively; for comparison, 5.7 ± 0.2 [mean ± s.e.m.], [N = 4], ripe banana; p = 0.0001; one-way ANOVA), known for its antioxidant properties.
evidence: Supported by pH measurements

claim: Banana is reported to contain up to 1 mg DA per gram of fresh weight.
source: Banana is reported to contain up to 1 mg DA per gram of fresh weight (Kanazawa and Sakakibara, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kanazawa and Sakakibara, 2000

claim: DA in banana is synthesized directly from TA.
source: Notably, DA in banana is synthesized directly from TA (Deacon and Marsh, 1971) and not via synthesis of l-DOPA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Deacon and Marsh, 1971

claim: The absence of l-DOPA in banana renders this non-host fruit unable to stimulate egg production in D. sechellia.
source: Presumably, the absence of l-DOPA in banana renders this non-host fruit unable to stimulate egg production in D. sechellia (see Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and biochemical knowledge

claim: Treatment with COMT suppressed the anti-apoptotic effects of morinda.
source: Treatment with COMT suppressed the anti-apoptotic effects of morinda (Figure 2B) and hindered the fruit from stimulating vitellogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and egg production in D. sechellia (Figure 2E), reducing the number of eggs to levels in a standard diet (compare Figure 2A and Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Treatment with COMT hindered morinda from stimulating vitellogenesis in D. sechellia.
source: Treatment with COMT suppressed the anti-apoptotic effects of morinda (Figure 2B) and hindered the fruit from stimulating vitellogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and egg production in D. sechellia (Figure 2E), reducing the number of eggs to levels in a standard diet (compare Figure 2A and Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment with COMT hindered morinda from stimulating egg production in D. sechellia.
source: Treatment with COMT suppressed the anti-apoptotic effects of morinda (Figure 2B) and hindered the fruit from stimulating vitellogenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and egg production in D. sechellia (Figure 2E), reducing the number of eggs to levels in a standard diet (compare Figure 2A and Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The presence of mDp in morinda strongly reduced egg production in D. sechellia.
source: Additionally, we added α-methyl-DOPA (mDp, 0.4 mM), a non-hydrolysable l-DOPA analogue and a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme dopa decarboxylase that converts l-DOPA into DA, separately to the fruit. The presence of mDp in morinda strongly reduced egg production (Figure 2E); feeding a corresponding mDp-supplemented diet to D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin did not have such an effect (not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: mDp in the fruit did not hinder oogenesis; instead, eggs were retained in the ovaries.
source: Notably, mDp in the fruit did not hinder oogenesis; instead, eggs were retained in the ovaries (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The halt in ovulation caused by mDp was completely reversed one day after flies were moved to fresh medium.
source: This halt in ovulation was completely reversed one day after flies were moved to fresh medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and, remarkably, oviposition was significantly enhanced when morinda was offered as an oviposition substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Oviposition was significantly enhanced when morinda was offered as an oviposition substrate after mDp treatment.
source: This halt in ovulation was completely reversed one day after flies were moved to fresh medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and, remarkably, oviposition was significantly enhanced when morinda was offered as an oviposition substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Morinda contains l-DOPA and its presence in the fruit pulp is both sufficient and necessary to stimulate egg production in D. sechellia.
source: We conclude that morinda contains l-DOPA and that its presence in the fruit pulp is both sufficient and necessary to stimulate egg production in D. sechellia.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with l-DOPA supplementation, COMT treatment, and mDp treatment

claim: Eggs of D. sechellia are characteristically large compared to those of sibling species.
source: An interesting observation provides one clue. Eggs of D. sechellia are characteristically large compared to those of sibling species D. melanogaster, D. simulans, Drosophila ananassae, Drosophila erecta, Drosophila mojavensis, Drosophila persimilis, Drosophila pseudoobscura, Drosophila virilis, Drosophila willistoni and Drosophila yakuba (Markow et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Markow et al., 2009

claim: D. sechellia eggs are 45% larger in size compared to eggs of D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin in a standard diet condition.
source: In accordance, we observed D. sechellia eggs to be 45% larger in size compared to eggs of D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin (Figure 3A), in a standard diet condition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Upon being fed a morinda diet, eggs of D. sechellia increased in volume twofold compared to eggs of conspecifics fed standard medium.
source: Upon being fed a morinda diet, eggs of D. sechellia increased in volume twofold compared to eggs of conspecifics fed standard medium (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1); the resulting eggs had an almost threefold larger volume than did D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin eggs in standard conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: D. sechellia eggs fed morinda diet had an almost threefold larger volume than did D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin eggs in standard conditions.
source: Upon being fed a morinda diet, eggs of D. sechellia increased in volume twofold compared to eggs of conspecifics fed standard medium (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1); the resulting eggs had an almost threefold larger volume than did D. melanogaster wild-type Berlin eggs in standard conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The effect of morinda on egg size could be replicated by supplementing standard diet with l-DOPA or DA.
source: This effect could be replicated by supplementing standard diet with l-DOPA or, notably, DA (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Adding COMT or mDp to a morinda diet prevented the fruit from having any effect on the volume of eggs.
source: On the other hand, adding COMT or mDp to a morinda diet prevented the fruit from having any effect on the volume of eggs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Egg size is under a dopaminergic control regime during egg development.
source: These results indicate that egg size is also under a dopaminergic control regime during egg development.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results with l-DOPA, DA, COMT, and mDp
